title: Life Is Water and Navigation
why: English describes life as a voyage across water: calm or stormy, shallow or deep. These idioms let you talk precisely about risk, struggle, change and letting go.
know: the conceptual metaphor LIFE IS A JOURNEY BY WATER and its link to the wider LIFE IS A JOURNEY
eight common idioms of water, depth, tides and boats
understand: the difference between being in deep water and being in hot water
why some idioms describe struggle, some describe progress and some describe change
able: describe difficulty, caution and turning points with idiomatic precision
choose between close pairs such as tread water and keep your head above water
talk about the past and moving on with water under the bridge
mistakes: After the scandal, the minister is in hot water financially.
The minister is in deep water financially. Hot water means trouble for doing wrong; deep water means serious difficulty.
That argument is water below the bridge.
That argument is water under the bridge. The preposition is fixed.
I felt out of my deep at the new job.
I felt out of my depth. The noun is depth.
Let's test the water of the market first.
Let's test the waters first. The idiom is usually plural and takes no of.
Don't shake the boat, the deal is almost done.
Don't rock the boat. Only rock works here.
bigidea: Lakoff and Johnson showed that English often treats LIFE IS A JOURNEY. When that journey is by water, we get a rich family of idioms: we navigate a career, steer a company, drift apart, and hope for plain sailing.

Water stands for forces we can't fully control. Its depth measures difficulty (out of your depth, in deep water), its movement stands for trends and change (go with the flow, turn the tide), and storms are crises we must weather.
For Canadians, with three oceans and the Great Lakes, these images are not abstract. The literal danger of water is what gives the metaphors their force.
hidden: We need someone to steer the project through the next phase.

expressions.meaning: try something carefully to see how people react before committing
expressions.example: The senator is testing the waters for a leadership run.
expressions.bend: Usually plural waters; test the water is also heard in Britain. Often test the waters for + noun.
expressions.note: Very common in politics and business. Near-synonym: dip a toe in the water, which suggests a small first step.

expressions.meaning: in a situation that is too difficult for your knowledge or ability
expressions.example: In the meeting with the tax lawyers, I felt completely out of my depth.
expressions.bend: Change the possessive: out of her depth, way out of our depth. Usually with be or feel.
expressions.note: From swimming where your feet can't touch the bottom. It's about ability, not about having too much work.

expressions.meaning: manage to survive, especially financially, but only just
expressions.example: With rent rising, many young families are struggling to keep their heads above water.
expressions.bend: Just about keep our heads above water, struggle to keep your head above water. Plural heads with plural subjects.
expressions.note: Focus is on survival. Compare tread water, which focuses on making no progress.

expressions.meaning: stay in the same position without making progress
expressions.example: The negotiations have been treading water since the spring.
expressions.bend: Any tense: we're just treading water, the economy trod water (or treaded). No article before water.
expressions.note: Usually mildly negative: you are busy but going nowhere.

expressions.meaning: change a situation, usually from bad to good
expressions.example: A late goal from the captain turned the tide in the final period.
expressions.bend: Turn the tide against/in favour of; also the tide is turning, stem the tide (stop a bad trend).
expressions.note: Popular with sports commentators and historians. Watch the difference: turn the tide changes direction, stem the tide only stops it.

expressions.meaning: cause trouble by challenging a stable situation
expressions.example: He had doubts about the policy but didn't want to rock the boat before his review.
expressions.bend: Usually negative: don't rock the boat, I didn't want to rock the boat. The wording is fixed.
expressions.note: Can praise or criticise: someone who never rocks the boat may be loyal or simply timid.

expressions.meaning: past problems that are forgotten or no longer matter
expressions.example: We fought a lot as teenagers, but that's all water under the bridge now.
expressions.bend: Usually it's (all) water under the bridge. A fixed phrase: don't change the preposition.
expressions.note: Signals forgiveness. Close to bury the hatchet, but that is an action; this describes the past.

expressions.example: If the loan isn't approved by Friday, the business will be in deep water.
expressions.bend: Get into deep water, be in deep water. Not usually plural.
expressions.note: Trap: in hot water means in trouble because you did something wrong and someone is angry. Deep water is just serious danger.

culture.how: The spirit Ariel sings to Ferdinand, who believes his father has drowned, describing how the sea has transformed the body into coral and pearls. This is where sea change comes from; today it means a complete, deep transformation.
culture.ask: What area of society has gone through a sea change in your lifetime?
culture.find: sea change The Tempest Ariel song meaning

culture.how: Before the final battle, Brutus argues that opportunity in human life works like the tide: catch it at its height and it carries you to success; miss it and you may be stranded in the shallows for the rest of your life. It is the classic picture behind turn the tide.
culture.ask: Have you ever caught, or missed, a high tide in your own life?
culture.find: Brutus tide in the affairs of men Julius Caesar

culture.how: A man dies in the sea and onlookers had assumed he was just waving and having fun. The poet turns this into a picture of someone who has struggled to keep their head above water all their life while everyone thought they were fine.
culture.ask: Why do people sometimes hide the fact that they are out of their depth?
culture.find: Stevie Smith Not Waving but Drowning

culture.how: Paul Simon's song uses the title image as a promise of loyalty: when a friend's life becomes dangerous and stormy, the singer offers to become the safe way across. Troubled water stands for any hard time.
culture.ask: Who has been a bridge over troubled water for you, or for whom have you been one?
culture.find: Simon and Garfunkel Bridge over Troubled Water

culture.work: The Wreck of the Edmund Fitzgerald
culture.how: The Canadian singer tells the true story of a freighter that sank in a storm on Lake Superior in November 1975, with all 29 crew lost. Here water is not a metaphor at all, and the song reminds us of the real danger behind phrases like weather the storm.
culture.ask: Does the literal danger of water make these idioms feel stronger to you? Which ones?

bend.q: Which version is a natural variation of turn the tide? ___
opts: The tide is finally turning for the team.
The tide is finally turned by the team's.
The tides finally turn the team.
bend.why: The tide is turning is a very common intransitive variation.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural about a whole family? ___
opts: We're just about keeping our head above waters.
We're just about keeping our heads above water.
We're just about keeping heads over water.
bend.why: Plural subject, plural heads; water stays singular and above is fixed.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural with an intensifier? ___
opts: I was way out of my depth.
I was out of my way depth.
I was out of my depths way.
bend.why: Way, completely or totally can go before out of your depth.

bend.q: Which version is a natural variation of test the waters? ___
opts: She's dipping a toe in the water with a part-time course.
She's dipping the waters with a part-time course.
She's testing a toe in the water with a part-time course.
bend.why: Dip a toe in the water is a close cousin of test the waters: a small first try.
